pr.body:
One potential problem we have with batch processing is that any one slow item will clog up the whole batch. This pr implements a queueing method instead, where we keep N queues that each have their own workers. There's still a chance of individual items backlogging a queue, but we can try increased concurrency here to reduce the chances of that happening

pr.title: feat(uptime): Add ability to use queues to manage parallelism

raw_findings.body: After the first rebalance, every subsequent submit() hits queue.ShutDown from work_queue.put(); the broad `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit marks the offset add_offset+complete_offset, so all messages are silently dropped while their offsets are committed — permanent data loss with no crash or backlog signal.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Consumer keeps running and committing offsets while processing nothing after the first rebalance, losing all subsequent results.
raw_findings.impact: After the first rebalance, every subsequent submit() hits queue.ShutDown from work_queue.put(); the broad `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit marks the offset add_offset+complete_offset, so all messages are silently dropped while their offsets are committed — permanent data loss with no crash or backlog signal.
raw_findings.root_cause: Pool ownership is split: the factory creates and reuses the FixedQueuePool across strategy generations, but the per-generation strategy destroys it in close()/terminate().
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Do not shut down the shared pool from the strategy's close()/terminate(); leave pool lifecycle to ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() (mirroring how parallel_executor is handled), or create a fresh FixedQueuePool per create_with_partitions call.
raw_findings.title: Strategy close() shuts down the factory-shared FixedQueuePool, causing silent message drops after any rebalance
raw_findings.trigger: Any consumer group rebalance or partition revocation: arroyo closes the current SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy (calling close()/join()) and then calls factory.create_with_partitions again, which reuses the same FixedQueuePool created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__. close() has already called queue.shutdown() on every pool queue and stopped every worker thread.

raw_findings.body: Queues grow without bound, retaining full WorkItem objects (including the original Kafka message payloads) and an ever-growing all_offsets/outstanding set, leading to memory exhaustion and OOM-kill of the consumer; the class docstring's guarantee 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' is false.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Unbounded memory growth under processing lag; consumer crashes instead of applying backpressure.
raw_findings.impact: Queues grow without bound, retaining full WorkItem objects (including the original Kafka message payloads) and an ever-growing all_offsets/outstanding set, leading to memory exhaustion and OOM-kill of the consumer; the class docstring's guarantee 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' is false.
raw_findings.root_cause: queue.Queue() is instantiated without maxsize and submit() has no overload path, while the docstring asserts backpressure exists.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Create queues with a maxsize and have SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit raise arroyo's MessageRejected (or block with timeout) when the target queue is full, so the stream processor applies backpressure and pauses consumption.
raw_findings.title: Worker queues are unbounded with no MessageRejected backpressure despite docstring claiming natural backpressure
raw_findings.trigger: Sustained period where result processing (DB lookups, Redis, Snuba production) is slower than Kafka consumption, or a single hot group backlogging one queue; submit() never blocks or raises MessageRejected, so arroyo keeps feeding messages.

raw_findings.body: Arroyo's commit closure and the underlying KafkaConsumer offset-staging state are mutated from two threads without synchronization, risking corrupted/staged-offset races, incorrect commits, or crashes in the stream processor that only appear under load.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Cross-thread mutation of non-thread-safe consumer/commit state producing intermittent offset corruption or crashes.
raw_findings.impact: Arroyo's commit closure and the underlying KafkaConsumer offset-staging state are mutated from two threads without synchronization, risking corrupted/staged-offset races, incorrect commits, or crashes in the stream processor that only appear under load.
raw_findings.root_cause: New _commit_loop thread calls the arroyo-provided commit function, which is only safe to call from the processing (main) thread.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Have _commit_loop only compute committable offsets into a shared structure, and invoke commit_function from the strategy's poll() method on the main consumer thread.
raw_findings.title: Commit callback invoked from background commit thread violates arroyo's single-threaded commit contract
raw_findings.trigger: Normal operation: the daemon commit thread wakes every second and calls commit_function (arroyo's Commit closure over the KafkaConsumer) concurrently with the main consumer thread executing poll()/pause()/resume() on the same consumer.

raw_findings.body: highest_committable never advances past the gap even though all delivered messages are processed; commits stall forever for that partition, consumer lag grows unbounded, and a restart reprocesses everything since the gap.
raw_findings.evidence: if offset in all_offsets and offset not in outstanding:
raw_findings.failure_mode: Permanent commit stall on any partition containing an offset hole, with silent lag growth.
raw_findings.impact: highest_committable never advances past the gap even though all delivered messages are processed; commits stall forever for that partition, consumer lag grows unbounded, and a restart reprocesses everything since the gap.
raw_findings.root_cause: get_committable_offsets treats Kafka offsets as a contiguous integer sequence, which is not guaranteed.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Track committability relative to offsets actually observed (e.g., commit up to the highest observed offset below the lowest outstanding one) instead of iterating a dense range(start, max_offset + 1) and requiring every integer offset to be present.
raw_findings.title: OffsetTracker assumes dense offsets; any gap in partition offsets permanently blocks commits past the gap
raw_findings.trigger: Non-contiguous offsets on the partition — e.g. transactional producer control records or log compaction — mean the missing offset is never delivered and never enters all_offsets, so the contiguity scan breaks at the gap on every commit tick.

raw_findings.body: The test encodes the opposite of the implemented semantics (failed messages ARE committed) and will intermittently fail on slow runs, producing flaky CI and masking the real at-most-once behavior on processing errors.
raw_findings.evidence: assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets
raw_findings.failure_mode: Timing-dependent flaky assertion that also documents incorrect expected behavior.
raw_findings.impact: The test encodes the opposite of the implemented semantics (failed messages ARE committed) and will intermittently fail on slow runs, producing flaky CI and masking the real at-most-once behavior on processing errors.
raw_findings.root_cause: Test asserts absence of a commit that the implementation performs asynchronously on a 1-second timer, so correctness depends on the test finishing before the timer fires.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite the assertion to match the intended semantics — either assert the failed offsets are eventually committed (deterministically waiting for the commit tick), or change the worker to not complete offsets on failure and then assert no commit occurs.
raw_findings.title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts offsets are not committed after failure, contradicting the implementation and passing only by timing
raw_findings.trigger: OrderedQueueWorker.run marks the offset complete in its `finally` block even when result_processor raises, so failed offsets become committable; the commit loop ticks every 1.0s. On a slow CI machine the test's polling loop (up to ~2s plus a 0.2s sleep) outlasts the first commit tick and committed_offsets gets populated.

validated_findings.root_cause: Test asserts absence of a commit that the implementation performs asynchronously on a 1-second timer, so correctness depends on the test finishing before the timer fires.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite the assertion to match the intended semantics — either assert the failed offsets are eventually committed (deterministically waiting for the commit tick), or change the worker to not complete offsets on failure and then assert no commit occurs.
validated_findings.title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts offsets are not committed after failure, contradicting the implementation and passing only by timing
validated_findings.trigger: OrderedQueueWorker.run marks the offset complete in its `finally` block even when result_processor raises, so failed offsets become committable; the commit loop ticks every 1.0s. On a slow CI machine the test's polling loop (up to ~2s plus a 0.2s sleep) outlasts the first commit tick and committed_offsets gets populated.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: The test at line 1922 asserts offsets are NOT committed after failure. Looking at the implementation, OrderedQueueWorker.run has a finally block that calls complete_offset (line 149 in context). However, the test's assertion 'len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets' could be correct if the commit loop hasn't ticked yet. The claim that this contradicts implementation requires proving the finally block runs on exception, but the test may be checking behavior before commit tick fires. Insufficient evidence of actual bug.

validated_findings.body: Rebalances and shutdowns can stall long past the requested timeout, risking max.poll.interval.ms violations that eject the consumer from the group and trigger cascading rebalances.
validated_findings.evidence:
def join(self, timeout: float | None = None) -> None:
        self.close()
validated_findings.failure_mode: Unbounded blocking in a code path arroyo expects to complete within the supplied timeout.
validated_findings.impact: Rebalances and shutdowns can stall long past the requested timeout, risking max.poll.interval.ms violations that eject the consumer from the group and trigger cascading rebalances.
validated_findings.root_cause: join() discards its timeout argument and delegates to close(), which uses fixed per-thread 5-second joins applied sequentially.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Honor the timeout parameter: divide the remaining deadline across the commit-thread join and worker joins (or join workers concurrently with a shared deadline) instead of fixed 5.0s per thread.
validated_findings.title: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join ignores the caller's timeout and can block far beyond it
validated_findings.trigger: Arroyo calls strategy.join(timeout) during rebalance/shutdown with a bounded timeout; close() joins the commit thread for up to 5s and FixedQueuePool.shutdown() joins each of num_queues workers sequentially for up to 5s each (e.g., 20 workers → up to 100s) while workers may still be draining non-immediate queue shutdowns.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Line 344-345 shows join(timeout) ignores the timeout parameter and just calls close(). close() at lines 335-338 joins commit_thread with 5.0s timeout, then calls queue_pool.shutdown() which joins each worker sequentially. With 20 workers (default), this could take 100+ seconds regardless of the timeout argument passed to join().
